articles.title: A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.
The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.
“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.
It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh , a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White . Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.
By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.
Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.
Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year .

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.
“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.
Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn .

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.
Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”
As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

articles.title: Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate .

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.
Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain , a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.
Ben Golden , an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax .
And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”
Brian Fioca , a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue . “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen , D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.
At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram .

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.
The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.
Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.
McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight . The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional , citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard .

articles.title: First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.
Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.
The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.
The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post . “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.
It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.
One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.
Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.
With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.
Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:
“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

articles.title: Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning , the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org , the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer , Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.
“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM , which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.
Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen , who started a climate modeling effort around 2016 at what was then known as Vulcan, his Seattle-based holding company. The group moved to Ai2 in 2021 , about two and a half years after his death. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.
In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models , called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.
Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.
Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.
Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

articles.title: Amazon plans its first data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Amazon is moving toward building its first data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities , with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings.
The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.
At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin . Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.
Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.
Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.
“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”
In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

articles.title: Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Seattle startup Finpilot , which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital , with participation from Madrona , which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan , Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.
“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round , Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.
“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.
Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.
In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg , co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.
Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.
What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.
Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

articles.title: Transit Measures Headed to Victory in Seattle, Pierce County
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Bus riders in Seattle and Pierce County are poised to see increased transit service in the wake of successful funding measures, with early returns showing strong voter support in both jurisdictions. Seattle's transit measure, which renews an existing sales tax measure supplementing King County Metro service, is ahead with 72.5% of the vote, while the funding measure for Pierce Transit is leading with a very respectable 57.7%.

Both propositions will bump up the local sales tax rate by 0.3% to fund bus service, with Seattle's measure set to enable nearly 100,000 more King County Metro bus trips every year on top of the 180,000 currently provided. It would also continue funding existing transit-related programs, including streetcar service and a major expansion of the number of subsidized ORCA transit cards provided by the City of Seattle.

Pierce Transit's measure will bump up service by nearly 50% compared to the levels seen today, expanding hours of operation and frequency across the entire network along with adding four brand new bus routes. It will also enable the agency to eliminate fares for seniors, building on the existing statewide free youth fare program.

A success at the ballot box in Seattle was all but assured, given the track record of the existing Seattle Transit Measure, which has been in place since 2014. The 2020 renewal passed with 80.3% of the vote , a nationwide record for a transit funding measure that has still never been surpassed. But for Pierce Transit, things were much less less certain in terms of going to the voters for more funding.

Serving Tacoma, Puyallup, Lakewood, University Place, Spanaway and Gig Harbor, Pierce Transit has been operating at a lower funding level than other peer agencies across the region for decades. A pair of defeated measures in 2011 and 2012 led to substantial service cuts and a contraction of the agency's total service area.
Those defeats ultimately led to a reluctance to head back to the ballot that was overcome this year, prompted by strong polling and high expected turnout during a midterm election.

The results are a major source of vindication for Pierce County's elected transit champions, including Tacoma City Councilmember Kristina Walker and Pierce County Executive Ryan Mello. Mello has been clear about the need to expand transit access in Pierce County since being elected in 2024, taking over after eight years of Republican leadership.

"For me, what it means is finally having a transit system that will connect more people to opportunity, to run their life and the essentials of their life," Mello told The Urbanist in an interview Wednesday morning. "So many of the things that I'm working on: connecting people to opportunity, connecting people to jobs, getting to school, after school programs to keep people safe, connecting vulnerable community members to healthcare and other services — the common barrier, time and time again, is transportation."

The 47% increase in service will be phased in by the early 2030s, ending the era of the hourly bus on the Pierce Transit network. The number of bus routes that operate every 30 minutes will jump from 18 to 24, with seven routes going to 15-20 minutes – frequency boosts that will represent a game changer for access across Pierce County.
Mello told The Urbanist that the 15-point margin on election night was a pleasant surprise.

"I was prepared for a much closer margin. I know we ran a really good campaign. I know we had a really clear message about what we were going to deliver, but you know, it's a tax measure in this economy, in this significant sense of uncertainty, there was a lot of concern about: would voters still be willing to invest in themselves and our community in this way," Mello said. "But they they surely see the value of making sure that more people can get access to opportunity, and I'm so proud of my neighbors for seeing the power of transit to connect more people to opportunity."

The passage of the Seattle Transit Measure Tuesday night notches a major win for Mayor Katie Wilson, who proposed doubling the existing 0.15% sales tax rate to 0.3%. Though that move was met with a hand-wringing over cost impacts that hasn't been seen with other sales tax bumps – including a 0.1% increase for public safety investments approved last year by her predecessor Bruce Harrell – Wilson made the case that increasing access to transit will outweigh the sales tax bump when it comes to the affordability impact for city residents.

"I just want to drive home the point that this is an affordability measure, and when gas is $6 a gallon, when the price of car ownership has never been higher, this measure – fast, frequent bus service, is going to allow more people, more households around our city, to get around on a most affordable mode of transportation," Wilson told transit supporters gathered at a Proposition 1 party in Pioneer Square. "And we are not going to stop until Seattle's transit system is irresistibly good."

Wilson was clearly in her element Tuesday night, with the win representing a full circle moment. Prior to being elected Mayor, Wilson led the Transit Riders Union, an organization that got its start advocating for transit funding in Seattle. In 2011, Wilson helped to launch the Save Our Metro! campaign to push against pending Metro service cuts stemming from the Great Recession. After those cuts were averted with a $20 car tab fee approved by the King County Council, the group pivoted to other transit fights including a push for a countywide low-income fare program.

"Seattle is not just a great transit city; it is the great transit city. And tonight shows us that that is still true," Wilson said. "This year has been a banner year for public transit in our city and our region. We've had some of the highest rebounding ridership in the country. We have opened up some of the most ambitious capital infrastructure anywhere in the U.S. We now have a light rail station that has the highest ridership of any light rail system in the whole entire country."
With the 2 Line now crossing Lake Washington, Sound Transit has surpassed 160,000 daily boardings, making it the most-ridden light rail system in the country.

With Seattle largely maxing out its transit funding capabilities with this renewal, attention is set to turn to King County Metro, which will be buoyed by this funding but still in need of a more sustainable long-term funding source to keep the agency stable. The millionaire's tax voters also upheld Tuesday means even less sales tax funding will be flowing into Metro's coffers at the end of this decade than had been expected, due to planned sales tax exemptions. King County Executive Girmay Zahilay will have to start to address a looming budget shortfall by next year's biennial budget.

"Seattle and King County residents deserve safe, affordable, and world-class transit. Renewing the Seattle Transit Measure reflects voters’ commitment to stronger, more connected communities by adding thousands of hours of Metro service, expanding early morning and late-night service, and providing free transit passes to more students, working families, and low-income residents," Zahilay said in a statement after the results dropped. "This historic investment will help Metro reach more communities and ensure more people have a sustainable, affordable, reliable way to get where they need to go."

The transit funding push across the region isn't even over. On Wednesday night, the Everett City Council will decide whether to give the green light for Community Transit to annex Everett Transit , trading away the city-specific 0.6% sales tax rate for Community Transit's 1.2%. That move will come with a 50% increase in transit service within the city by 2031, and transit connections that simply can't exist with Snohomish County's largest city maintaining a completely separate transit agency.
Wednesday's vote will be followed by a vote of the Community Transit board on Thursday.

Thanks to a 2025 change in state law, Everett Transit's annexation will be able to happen without the voters directly weighing in. But the move represents a bold swing by three-term Everett Mayor Cassie Franklin, who has been making the case that the city can't grow sustainably without making substantial investments in transit.

Earlier this year, voters in and around Spokane also signed onto a 0.2% sales tax measure that will allow Spokane Transit to maintain existing service and grow in the future. Clearly, the momentum is on the side of transit expansion in 2026 in Washington State.

articles.title: Why a Seattle Electric Vehicle Charging Lot Is Taking Half a Decade to Build
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: How long does it take to build eight parking stalls? For Seattle City Light, the answer to that question remains a moving target.

Since 2022, Seattle City Light (SCL) has been trying to build a surface parking lot for electric vehicle charging in West Seattle's Morgan Junction neighborhood, on a former substation that had been sitting decommissioned for 20 years. The 4,500-square-foot site is set to see eight paid, fast-charging stations, which City Light touts as bringing EV charging "closer to neighborhood retail, services, and major arterial roads in Morgan Junction." But the project has faced numerous setbacks, with the publicly owned utility recently firing its contractor in the middle of construction.

Even in a city where timelines for public works projects often stretch longer than originally promised, the Morgan Junction charging lot has become a symbol of frustration with local government being able to deliver on promises. When the project was launched in 2022, City Light noted that construction could begin as soon as that year, and take approximately three months. Now, the lot doesn't look poised to open until September of 2027.

The West Seattle Blog has studiously chronicled the long saga of the Morgan Junction charging lot over its years of planning and development, either directly or by covering updates at monthly meetings of the Morgan Community Association. That reporting has shown timelines that continued to slip as the project advanced through design, even before being beset by issues during construction.

"Morgan Junction is our largest and most ambitious EV-charging station project to date requiring more time, engineering, and permitting than one of our more typical EV charging station projects," a former SCL spokesperson told the WSB in late 2024 , when the lot was still in design. "We’ve also experienced significant delays with procurement of the chargers and other electric service equipment. This is likely due to the rapid increase in transportation electrification costs nationwide."

In early 2025, District 1 Councilmember Rob Saka announced that his office had taken "decisive steps" to "accelerate the timeline" for the project, publishing an internal SCL memo laying out a schedule that would allow the city to start construction that October. But it wasn't until February of this year that contractor Zenisco Inc. did actually start work.

Five months later, construction work was halted on the site after the city found an issue: the east wall of the site needed a redesign due to work-quality issues and site conditions, in order to maintain the barrier between the lot and the adjacent alleyway.

"While crews worked on site during the FIFA construction moratorium, City Light construction engineers identified a significant structural design issue," SCL said in an update to the West Seattle Blog in July . "This required a complete work stoppage and will further delay the project so the project team can develop a solution. We will provide an estimated completion date for the charging station once the solution is approved by permitting authorities."
Just a few weeks later, after the design issue was resolved, SCL fired Zenisco, a decision that looked to stem from those aforementioned site quality issues.

"This project has taken longer than we planned, and we understand the frustration that comes with that. We’re committed to completing this work and opening the station for the Morgan Junction and all who visit," SCL posted in an update to the project website in September.

As of that time, the City was still waiting on next steps when it came to securing a new contractor, but did set the new completion date of September of 2027. Another schedule slip likely wouldn't shock anyone following this project, however.

The Morgan Junction site is far from the only site where City Light has run into issues implementing a standalone EV charging lot. In 2021, SCL proposed to convert another decommissioned substation along NW Market Street in Ballard to a charging lot, but backed off after doing early planning work.

"A soil test determined that on-site drainage options would not work and the only viable drainage option was to install a connection to the municipal stormwater sewer on the south side of NW Market Street," a 2022 SCL update on that project stated. "Seattle City Light decided that the added cost and disruption to vehicle traffic and King County Metro trolley bus operations on NW Market Street made this project unviable. Seattle City Light may resume work if a less disruptive method of providing site drainage is found."

After abandoning that project, SCL turned its attention to a site in Belltown , a leftover parcel owned by the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). Originally eyed as a spot for a potential public playground as part of the Waterfront Park redevelopment, a potential land swap for a nearby SCL property on the future site of Portal Park opened up the opportunity for EV charging.

In the face of significant concerns about using such a high-value site near Pike Place Market as another surface parking lot, SCL abandoned that project as well, citing "unforeseen delays and funding constraints."
For now, City Light appears to be pivoting away from the idea of building more standalone lots, according to SCL spokesperson Kate Jacobs.
"Our planned expansion does not include comparable sites that would require new lots," Jacobs wrote via email.

The utility has had much more success in adding curbside charging in the public right-of-way, aiming for 200 on-street charging locations by 2030 via funding from the 2024 Seattle Transportation levy.
And as for the Morgan Junction lot, where work is expected to soon resume? Jacobs said that SCL will be learning from its stumbles there as soon as the ribbon is cut.

"We will conduct a comprehensive review of all phases of the project as soon as we’ve delivered this important asset to the community," Jacobs wrote. "Implementing lessons learned is part of our standard process, and lessons from Morgan Junction and past projects will improve how we deliver public charging as we expand our network to meet growing demand."

articles.title: Conservatives Take Their Swings as 2026 Election Trends Toward Progressives
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Right-wing extremism had been having a moment, but tonight's election could be a major setback against that push and a leftward shift for the United States – at least if polling is on the mark. While polls have been positive for Democrats, right-wing leaders are not taking this lying down. In fact, the wealthy elite are spending at unprecedented levels.

Elon Musk alone has poured nearly a half billion dollars into the midterm elections, hoping to keep Republicans in power and hold back a blue wave. As the world's richest person, Musk obviously has an interest in continuing Trump tax cuts, shielding his personal and corporate wealth and lining up further political favors for his companies.

Some of Washington state's wealthiest people are also looking to influence elections in a big way. Hedge fund manager Brian Heywood is leading the way with his three statewide initiatives that will strip rights from queer students, require genital inspections for female athletes, and block the state's new millionaires tax, which is set to go into effect in 2029.

With Washington voters increasingly backing Democrats and giving them a strong trifecta in Olympia, uberwealthy conservatives increasingly are getting creative in their attempts to control political outcomes, spending millions on signature gathering efforts to force initiatives onto the ballot to repeal laws or pass new ones. Beyond the statewide measures, Heywood and his conservative cronies are looking to restructure Snohomish County government to make it easy for conservatives to veto progress, even when in a legislative minority.

Corporate elites are getting into the act, too. Microsoft and other top companies put together a Washington Need to Compete political action committee (PAC) with a huge war chest. So far, the PAC has run an ad criticizing the direction in Olympia during two primetime Seahawks football games. Washington Observer 's Paul Query reported that Washington Need to Compete has amassed $14 million, but has spent only $3 million, keeping most in reserve for 2027.

"[The ads are] intended as a warning shot to the Legislature and Gov. Bob Ferguson, and it seems to have pissed the latter right off," Query wrote. "Last week, at the Seattle Chamber’s Regional Leadership Conference, a schmoozy affair held out at the Suncadia resort, Ferguson teed off on the Redmond-based software behemoth."
The ad struck a nerve, with Ferguson bringing up that the state was smashing records for venture capital investment in startups.

"If we're partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right," Ferguson said in the recording. "If I ran some multi-million-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft for some things, you guys all would think I've lost my mind."

Ferguson continued to extend an olive branch, even as he questioned the communication style Microsoft and friends were using. He also cast doubt on the threat they appeared to be trying to deliver that they could dislodge him with big campaign spending to propel a political challenger from the right, adding he planned on being governor for a "long time."

"Washington State sure as heck as a government can do more and do better by all of you folks and all the workers you represent, but it works both ways, right?" Ferguson told the chamber crowd. "It works both ways, and so that's what I would say: I plan on being governor for a long time. I work with all of you, Microsoft included, who I work well with. But I do have some questions about how we communicate."

Microsoft targeting Ferguson is a bit surprising since he's operated as a centrist and taken pains to push for budget cuts over new taxes. Even though Ferguson ultimately signed the millionaires tax , he quickly pivoted to saying it was time for budget cuts after setting the new tax in motion, which will take several years to bring in revenue given its long implementation runway.

The millionaires tax clearly is high on the list of policy changes angering the corporate establishment. One of the legislative races that the Microsoft-funded PAC has spent most heavily is the state senate race in the 48th Legislative District, where more union-backed, left-leaning Redmond Mayor Jessica Forsythe is seeking to unseat Senator Amy Walen, who was one of the few votes against the millionaires tax in the Democratic caucus. The PAC has spent more than $700,000 defending her. Clearly, the ultrarich do not want to see Walen go.

While millionaires worry about slightly higher tax bills, many Americans have growing concerns about covering basic necessities and making ends meet as Trump's war in Iran drags on, driving up fuel prices. Trump's tariff regime is also driving up consumer prices, taking money out of families' pockets while alienating allied nations.

Health care workers and advocates under the banner of the Healthcare and Human Rights Coalition held a rally in Renton last week to demand universal health care. A chorus of speakers made the case, noting that Trump's actions were driving up health care costs for many Americans by kicking people off Medicaid and disrupting insurance marketplaces that had moderated costs.

King County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda, who is up for reelection and is endorsed by The Urbanist Elections Committee (on which I serve), spoke at the rally, saying a crisis also brings opportunity.

"Now is the time for action. Don't waste a crisis," Mosqueda said. "We know that other countries with similar GDP, similar economies, similar capitalist mentalities have already committed to healthcare as a human right, and that's why we're demanding universal healthcare for all. And we're not here to wait for the cavalry to come from the feds. We're not here to wait to make sure that the D.C. folks can hear us and take action to repeal H.R. 1. We're here to call for action right here in Washington State, right here in King County."

Speakers decried work requirements that Trump added to Medicaid as part of H.R. 1, which could lead to millions more being uninsured and without health care access. In addition to harming those in poverty, health care policy changes also put women and trans people at risk.

Jaelynn Scott, who is running unopposed for the state House in the 37th Legislative District, with The Urbanist's endorsement . Scott is executive director of the Lavender Rights Project, a national Black trans feminist organization advancing justice for gender diverse communities, and noted a proxy way was going on targeting the bodies of LGBTQ people.

"I want to [give a] thank you to the Healthcare and Human Rights Coalition for organizing this gathering as we watch the Trump administration give billionaires tax cuts and pass through costs to our state," Scott said. "We're sitting aside and waiting on action from our state legislature. Look, the billionaires and Trump administration are playing proxy wars on our bodies. Nowhere, nowhere is that more evident than with the communities that I organize with – that's LGBTQ communities, the communities that I'm running to represent in the 37th."
Scott alluded to Republican increasing attacks on trans people as a means to fire up their base despite failures and broken promises on other issues.

"They are attacking specifically trans communities and stripping our health care," Scott said. "So, now we're in the position as a state that we have to do Medicaid backfill, and we're going to do the bare minimum. But we have to do more than the bare minimum. How can we ensure that we show that Washington State is a state that actually is a sanctuary for all, and that healthcare is a human right, and that gender-affirming care is great in this state?"

If Democrats succeed nationally in retaking Congress, repealing H.R. 1 would be a bold goal, but one within their reach. Barring action, health care will become increasingly unaffordable for working families and some will lack access altogether.

articles.title: County adjusts Broadway crisis center construction budget to $35M as facility plans take shape
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: King County Public Health is addressing rising cost projections for its planned Central Crisis Care Center on Broadway, telling CHS that a newly proposed $35 million budget request reflects refined project requirements, not cost overrun.

The county acquired the former Polyclinic building at 1110 Harvard Ave for $41.5 million to create a 24/7 walk-in behavioral health facility. An early renovation estimate of $16 to 17 million in early discussions around the project was a preliminary “Rough Order of Magnitude” figure, according to a spokesperson.

That initial projection accounted only for hard construction expenses, omitting soft costs such as engineering, architectural design, permitting, and owner contingencies before operational programming with designated operator Connections Health Solutions had begun.

To keep the redevelopment on track for a targeted late-2027 opening, the County Facilities Management Division has requested a $35 million authorization, funded by rebalancing the voter-approved Crisis Care Centers Levy implementation budget.
Final construction figures and schematic designs will be released once a general contractor joins the team early next year, the spokesperson said.

Officials also confirmed that the property’s vacant southern lot will be addressed. After building renovations are fully designed, the county will consult neighbors and the City of Seattle on potential uses, including community-requested green space.

CHS reported here last month on the beginning of a key land use review process for the facility for interior and exterior upgrades that “apply the principles of trauma-informed design, and recognize the unique needs of individuals across the lifespan” at the medical building on the edge between First Hill and Capitol Hill.
The new construction outlook would push the total price tag on the project above $76 million for the acquisition and transformation of the three-story building.

A citizen-led Seattle Community Advisory Group formed to help shape planning for the project is also working to allocate an additional $3 million county mitigation fund to address street disorder and public safety gaps.
CHS reported on the advisory group’s early work around public safety improvements focused heavily on surrounding street conditions.

articles.title: Election Night on Capitol Hill: ‘late voter’ drop-box lines, big transit win, and split trans initiative counts
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The long lines at the Broadway ballot drop box were testament. Voter enthusiasm for progressive policies and candidates willing to fight for them was high on Election Night as national victories connected to important decisions here at home. And, yes, even when the stakes are high, “late voters” ruled on Capitol Hill.

On E Pike, organizers from No Hate in Washington State gathered at Neumos on Capitol Hill to watch the first results come in on the two statewide initiatives the coalition was created to stand against. Back in February , CHS talked with organizer Danni Askini of the Capitol Hill-based Gender Justice League about the effort that grew to lead the statewide fight.

Initiative 001 sought to enforce parental rights measures regarding public school curriculum review, record access, and parental notifications for student health services while Initiative 638 would prohibit transgender girls from participating in women’s school sports and institute biological sex verification requirements for student athletes.
Election Night’s first count showed a split on the hoped-for “no” results with organizers pinning hopes on later voters to close the gap on 638.
Meanwhile, the votes for the State Senate race in the 43rd District representing the area including most of Capitol Hill fell along lines similar to the primary.

Two-decade incumbent State Sen. Jamie Pedersen produced a 67% showing in August winning precincts across Capitol Hill and most of the 43rd District save for a few blocks of central Broadway where first-time challenger and “Tax the Rich” proponent Hannah Sabio-Howell managed a flat-footed tie.

Pedersen’s November election victory will take on similar proportions. CHS reported here on the funding surge behind Pedersen, the party’s current Majority Leader in the state Senate, an architect of the Millionaires Tax , and a veteran lawmaker who has been part of 43rd District leadership for twenty years, as state Democratic leaders helped lock down the race so institutional donors and statewide PACs could shift their war chests to competitive general election battlegrounds elsewhere in the state.
Statewide, voters were also roundly rejecting an initiative to repeal Pedersen’s Millionaires Tax.

“A big win for working families,” Pedersen said in a statement. “Last night, we celebrated the decisive defeat of Initiative 645 and reaffirmed what Washingtonians deserve: an economy that works for everyone, not just the wealthiest few.”

For Seattle voters, the decision was apparently easy on the the 2026 Seattle Transit Measure and its proposed 10-year renewal funded by a 0.3% sales tax championed by Mayor Katie Wilson to allow the city to purchase increased bus service on key routes.
The Election Night first count tallied nearly 73% support for the tax increase.

“With this vote, Seattle voters are once again generously investing in building a transit system that is convenient to use, affordable to access, and that easily connects them to opportunity and prosperity,” Wilson said in a statement. “Seattle is already a great transit city, and this measure will deliver the largest expansion of transit service in our city’s history, double the low-income transit passes available to Seattleites, and provide resources for faster and more reliable service.”

Officials say the tax bump will expand Seattle’s capacity from 180,000 to 280,000 annual bus trips — a 47% increase in total service. The plan boosts frequencies on 10 to 15 key routes, expands late-night and weekend service, and prioritizes electric buses in South Seattle and the Duwamish Valley. The measure will “double the number of free ORCA cards provided to low-income households” by expanding subsidized passes to 12,000 additional residents, while allocating funds to “support the recommendations of the King County Regional Transit Safety Task Force.”
Voter turnout totals early on Election Night

Meanwhile, voters in North Seattle are making a choice that could shift the makeup of the Seattle City Council . First counts show progressive advocate Nilu Jenks besting educator Julie Kang for the District 5 seat on the council.

Beyond the 43rd District Senate contest and the transit measure, Capitol Hill and Central District voters weighed in on federal representation for Washington’s 7th Congressional District, multiple state legislative seats across both the 43rd and 37th districts spanning both House positions and the 37th District Senate seat, and countywide races including King County Prosecuting Attorney, King County Assessor, and King County Council District 2 where State Senator Rebecca Saldaña held a strong lead over Port Commissioner Toshiko Hasegawa for the seat.

Ballots also included Seattle Municipal Court judicial seats. Many candidates ran unopposed or faced longshot challengers. Capitol Hill and Central District voters also filled in the bubbles in several key statewide judicial races.

Voter turnout in King County was trending high with Seattle as a whole just over 48% by early Election Night. That number will surely climb with District 3 and Capitol Hill’s classic surge of “late voters.”
Results will continue to roll in from Washington’s by-mail and by-drop box election over the coming day. You can view all the numbers at results.votewa.gov .

articles.title: Seattle Council budget plan raids JumpStart to reverse mayor’s cuts but backs off police hiring boost
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The Seattle City Council has released its initial package of changes to Mayor Katie Wilson’s proposed 2027–2028 city budget , tapping $31 million in JumpStart payroll tax reserves and cutting $22 million in pension transfers to reverse cuts proposed by the mayor. Like the mayor’s plan, the council’s Balancing Package would also keep Seattle out of deficit through 2030 — but it would do so by digging into funding the mayor had sought to protect.

The package released Wednesday also incorporates amendments from District 3 representative Council President Joy Hollingsworth directing funds to community reinvestment, family shelter operations, tenant protections, and neighborhood cultural programming.

The proposal from Select Budget Committee Chair Dan Strauss serves as the council’s rewrite of the executive budget. Both plans leave the city’s official Emergency Subfund and Revenue Stabilization Fund untouched, but they use different methods to get to a balanced budget.

“We have built momentum addressing some of our most serious issues. We can’t stop now,” Strauss said about efforts to reverse public safety-related cuts and restore funding for firefighter overtime. “This proposal will help us maintain momentum without cuts to essential services that keep people safe and help make Seattle more affordable.”

The Council’s Balancing Package focuses on emergency response by restoring a proposed $7.1 million annual cut to the Seattle Fire Department’s overtime budget, providing $1 million in 2027 to repair the fireboat Leschi, and restoring five civilian Seattle Police Department investigator positions to assist detectives with homicide, robbery, and gun crime caseloads. In addition to funding two non-emergency 911 dispatchers in the CARE department, the package restores nine parking enforcement officers, allocates $300,000 across two years for suppressed patrol rifles, and commissions a $100,000 study on creating a regional fire protection district while reducing General Fund transfers to the Fire Pension Fund by $22 million over the biennium to help balance the overall budget.

Notably, the package being carried forward by the council sidesteps the debate over police hiring. One proposal had called for adding nearly $800,000 next year and $11.6 million in 2028 to accelerate hiring to 12 recruits per month, aiming for 135 net new officers over the next two years, unwinding the mayor’s attempts to save millions by downshifting the process. That proposed amendment did not make the council’s initial package.

In total, the council adds about $41 million in restored and new spending across the biennium. Key citywide additions include $5 million added to housing, $7.1 million over two years for vehicle residency programs and a second safe RV lot, and $1.5 million to help the City Attorney clear criminal case backlogs and hire two assistant prosecutors.
The RV homelessness program spending is at the center of another Strauss clash with Wilson after the mayor’s veto of the legislation setting up a parking permit program for RV campers.
A significant portion of the council’s package reflects priorities from Hollingsworth, who is the lead sponsor on several proposed investments:
To pay for the broader additions while leaving the city’s emergency and rainy day accounts untouched, the council pacakge relies on special funds and spending shifts:

Seattle leaders including former Mayor Bruce Harrell have leaned heavily on revenue from the city’s JumpStart tax on its largest employers to patch spending holes. As originally legislated, the payroll tax’s flexibility to contribute to General Fund spending was intended to sunset in 2025 so the revenue could be fully dedicated to the program’s original affordable housing and social services funding goals.

The Select Budget Committee will discuss the package Wednesday morning.. A public hearing takes place Thursday, November 5th with remote comment at 1 PM and in-person comment at 5 PM . Council members will submit further amendments before committee voting starts on November 13th.

articles.title: Mixed use: You probably won’t be surprised by what the Capitol Hill corner once home to Piecora’s is set to become
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Capitol Hill is dead. First, Microsoft killed it. Then, Amazon .

Early paperwork shows that a key corner in the great wave of 2010s redevelopment that shaped modern Capitol Hill is about to go back into motion with a business at 14th and Madison for the first time since the legendary Piecora’s Pizza served its final slices in 2014 .
Permits have been filed for a massive new pilates studio on the corner from the BODYROK franchise chain.

The business will be the first ever tenant of the street level commercial suites of the Chloe on Madison mixed-use development since the Ankrom Moisan Architects -designed project opened seven years ago.

Through its long wait for a tenant, the largest of the long-empty suites has been marketed as an ideal location for a ground-up restaurant project but BODYROK is making plans for a 3,280-square-foot studio in the space.

The ghosts of Piecora’s might be long gone by the time it opens. National developer Equity Residential purchased the 14th and Madison pizza property from the Piecora family in spring of 2014 for a whopping $10.3 million. Debra and Daniel Piecora paid $3 million to purchase the property twelve years earlier. Soon after the Equity sale, Piecora’s announced its final day. The old pizza joint and the rest of the commercial buildings on the block were demolished in 2015 . The block then sat empty for a couple years before construction began and the new mixed-use apartment building finally opened in 2019.
Now, the block is finally set to have business activity again along this stretch of E Madison.

Across the street, the Tanager Apartments , a rare mixed-use construction project in the current inflation-throttled development environment in the city, has popped up, rising above the cluster of music clubs and bars it was designed to puzzle-piece around. Chop Suey , the Madison Pub , and 14th Ave bear bar Diesel remained open during the construction.
Meanwhile, Capitol Hill may not be completely dead. The Tanager’s first commercial tenant is lined up to be this coffee and cocktails project .

As for Piecora’s and BODYROK, the unlikely pairing of space if not time is part of one of the strange new directions for life on Capitol Hill. Over on 15th Ave E, the location formerly home to the equally legendary Canterbury Tavern is being readied for a MOOV movement and fitness studio.

Swapping red-sauce institutions like Piecora’s and the Canterbury for boutique fitness might read like a heavy-handed punchline, but seven years of dark storefronts is a long time to wait. As fitness studios take over beloved old taprooms and pizza corners across the neighborhood, Capitol Hill isn’t dead. It’s just sweating through another identity shift, this time, one high-rent square foot at a time.

articles.title: Months after surviving shooting outside E Pike club, hip hop artist gunned down in Burien
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: A fatal shooting in Burien has connections to E Pike where victim Marquise Johnson-Goldsmith had previously survived a shooting just months earlier.
Johnson-Goldsmith, a 26-year-old musical artist who performed as Godz Child , died early Sunday, October 25th after suffering a gunshot wound to the neck in a Burien parking lot.

In May , Johnson-Goldsmith survived being shot three times outside Capitol Hill nightclub Cultura in an incident that left three wounded and led to first-degree assault charges against a Tacoma teenager.
The victim’s mother is asking witnesses to come forward.
King County Sheriff detectives are investigating.

articles.title: Idaho Voters Picked the Evilest Possible State Gun
articles.author: Hunter Pauli
paras: Despite the best efforts of the Idaho Republican Party, the state’s people still have the right to propose citizen initiatives, which appear on the ballot alongside initiatives referred by the far-right state Legislature. For instance, Idaho residents this year voted down a grassroots attempt to restore abortion access, as well as a ploy by the Legislature to forever curb marijuana legalization by giving the legislature sole power over the matter.

Those are issues that actually matter which will be dissected by politicos in the weeks and months to come. But I want to talk about the stupidest thing on the Idaho ballot: House Bill 932, which the Legislature placed on the ballot to give We the People the opportunity to choose which firearm should be the official state gun of Idaho.

At the very least we can be happy that Idaho legislators picked six old boomer firearms made of wood and heavy steel rather than some gross modern plastic AR-15 or Glock facsimile (maybe a 3D-printed ghost gun would best reflect Idaho politics, or a Nazi Luger).

These are all proud made-in-America chud guns. The 1894 Winchester’s innovative smokeless cartridges made it great for putting down labor actions in the Pacific Northwest, including the left-wing mining union uprisings that state and federal forces suppressed in 1890s North Idaho multiple times with another new military innovation: concentration camps .

The 1873 Winchester is described on the ballot as “the gun that won the West,” a euphemistic whitewash for our long genocide of the Indigenous peoples beyond the Mississippi (if you ever want to feel really cynical, look up what the Union Army was doing in the Pacific Northwest during the Civil War). The Single Action Army revolver carries much the same reputation, while the Remington 700 is a deer hunting rifle so beloved by outdoorsmen that the US military has used them to snipe people across the globe for decades.

Speaking of sniping, in the grand tradition of pointless leftwing infighting, I must critique the rational of the South Idaho branch of the Democratic Socialists of America for its endorsement of the Colt 1911 for its supposed anti-fascist merits as the sidearm of choice of American troops in World War II.

While South Idaho DSA is correct that the 1911 was a “weapon against fascism” in WWII, it was also a tool of futile butchery in World War I and related American imperial misadventures, such as our efforts to snuff out the Mexican Revolution. Their assessment of the year 1911 being “the year that the first socialist was elected in Idaho” would also be news to those 1890s radical miners whose elected Populist Party local government was overthrown by the US military. As anyone in North Idaho will tell you, the city slickers down in Boise are always a little out of touch with Panhandle politics, socialists included.

Pound for pound the M1 Garand rifle did more to liberate North Africa and Western Europe from Axis fascism than the humble 1911, but it placed dead last in Idaho’s election (behind the 1911). A reflection of Idaho’s far-right politics? The stakes are low enough that it’s a conclusion I’m willing to jump to. The M1, of course, also has a dirty postwar history. As a rifle mass-produced to win a world war, the US government has used its vast surplus to arm everyone from the doomed Army of the Republic of Vietnam to modern Haitian cops.

That’s the problem with choosing to honor a firearm in the first place. Killing machines are inherently problematic things. Like most elections, the choice for voters came down to selecting the least worst option, and as they often do, Idaho voters picked the worst one: the Winchester 1873.
