articles.title: Slog AM: Democrats Take Congress, Millionaires Tax Stays, Trans Sports Ban Could Pass
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Goodbye Republican Congress! Try not to let the tsunami hit you on the way out. Oops! It hit you? Hm. Maybe that’s because you did zero to help Americans with basic problems—food prices, gas prices, housing prices, the list goes on and on—while at the same time opening the door and laying yourselves down as eager doormats for a cabal of corrupt He Man cosplayers who started a war, broke their promises on the Epstein Files, and spent a stunning amount of their time telling us all that the wannabe emperor was well clothed.

We woke up with that special, slightly dizzy feeling that comes from sampling too many mojitos at the Nilu Jenks party up in Ravenna, listening to the mayor ask permission to curse (permission granted now and forever, your honor!), and mainlining at least three airhorn blasts. So while the incoming Democratic majorities in DC are (hopefully!) preparing to make good on their cost-of-living promises and smartly wield their new subpoena power, let’s turn to what Election Day brought us here in Seattle and around the Pacific Northwest:

A Dem supermajority in Olympia: Democrats needed to pick up seven more seats in the House and three more seats in the Senate to gain a supermajority in Olympia. As things stand right now, the Dems are up in nearly all those important races.

In Washington State Supreme Court land: For the most part, the more progressive judicial candidates are running away with this thing. Colleen Melody, former head of the civil rights division at the attorney general’s office and current justice, left tax attorney Scott Edwards in the dust, winning 60 percent of the vote. It’s the same story with former ACLU attorney and current King County Superior Court Judge Jaime Michelle Hawk and Antonin Scalia fan and Mason County Superior Court Judge David Stevens. Hawk secured 57 percent. It’s a closer contest, but not by much, between former lawyer and current justice Theo Angelis and retired Federal Way Municipal Court judge and staunch Republican Dave Larson, with Angelis winning 55 percent to Larson’s 44 percent. Chief Justice Debra Stephens will be allowed to keep up the good work. She won 64 percent of the vote. The only close race is between Washington State Court of Appeals Judge Ian Birk and King County Superior Court Judge Sean O’Donnell who have 49 percent and 51 percent, respectively. The later returns should be more progressive, which could help Birk since O’Donnell is the more conservatively-aligned judge.

What does this mean? Voters clearly do not want a referendum on the courts and do not want to see Republicans get their sticky fingers on any branch of government in this state, no matter how much money conservatives funnel into a low-information race. This bodes well for the future of the Millionaires Tax as it faces down its next challenge: a legal fight that will eventually lead to our state supreme court justices weighing in on the constitutionality of the Millionaires Tax (and income taxes in general) in Washington State.

Speaking of those initiatives: Voters rejected the Millionaires Tax repeal and the resurrection of the bad Parents’ Bill of Rights, but the trans sports ban is still alive. We’ll have to keep an eye on the next ballot drops to see if voters really are this dumb and transphobic.

But we also elected the first openly trans state legislator in Washington: Jaelynn Scott won 87 percent of the vote last night. She’s the first Black trans legislator to hold office in the US. Scott will join Shaun Scott as the second socialist in the halls of Olympia (note: you do not need to have the last name Scott to be a socialist representative). Here she is speaking to Hasan Piker:
Seattle loves transit: The Seattle Transit Measure passed handily with nearly 73 percent of city voters approving it. Seattle fucking loves the bus.
Pierce County loves the bus, too: Our neighbors down south approved their own transit measure. That will give them a 47 percent increase in bus service.

In city news: Seattle’s District 5 finally elected a progressive to the city council. Nilu Jenks, the political and partnerships director with FairVote Washington, looks like she’ll be kicking Deborah Juarez (who was appointed to fill Cathy Moore’s seat) off the dais once and for all. Jenks won 58.5 percent of the vote last night, beating out Julie Kang. If these results hold—and they should—Jenks will take office later this month and provide a crucial progressive voice to the council and help with Mayor Katie Wilson’s agenda.

The stock market? It’s apparently cheering last night’s results, which were a disaster for the leader of MAGA. Presently, the Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 1,000 points . Analysts at CNBC interpret the surge as a result of the Dems’ clear victory, which makes it difficult, if not impossible, for Trump to stir his usual political chaos. But the markets were also never pleased about Trump’s imperial tariffs. They put a real drag on the economy, which has probably been in recession since late last year. So it’s very likely that the investor class sees the Dems control of both houses as a potential check on Trump’s ability to wake up and declare insanely sensational tariff hikes on Truth Social.

Now that Trump has been deflated , we need to turn to our next big problem: Moderate Dems! Already, there’s this talk by Hakeem Jefferies , the next speaker of the house , about looking forward not backward. No. We need to look back and fix a whole bunch of shit. It’s not about retribution. That’s not the right word. It’s about the nuts and bolts of our democracy, which Trump removed and tossed willy-nilly on the floor. You can’t give this monster one more inch after today. Remember, the biggest concern among American voters, according to Fox, was not the price of gas or groceries but corruption . Looking only forward means not dealing with this mountain of corruption that’s right behind us.

Idaho voters reject restoration of abortion rights: They lost them to a trigger law when the US Supreme Court released its Dobbs decision, and progressive organizers fought an uphill battle against the farthest-right state Republican Party in the Northwest to get reproductive rights back on the ballot. The polling was good, with most Idahoans supporting abortion rights, but the campaign failed big time, 44-56 at latest count. This suggests a failure of organization on supporters’ side, a failure to mobilize, and that ultimately, for now, Idaho’s gonna Idaho.

Blue wave saves doomed Oregon governor: Tina Kotek was polling dismally, but secured a second term last night. Her strategy? If you’re unpopular, find someone even more unpopular to bully, in this case President Trump.

Blue wave didn’t save Florida. MAGA republicans survived strong challenges from the left. Byron Donalds will become the Sunshine State’s governor, and Ashley Moody, who faced DSA’s Angie Dixon , will fill the senate seat left by Marco Rubio. It looks like Florida will become a permanent bunker for America’s billionaires.

Alaska’s Senate seat is too close to call: Democratic challenger Mary Peltola leads incumbent Republican Dan. S Sullivan 48.18-47.88 by latest count, less than 700 votes. We have to include Sullivan’s middle initial because Democrats recruited a doppelganger of his to run in this race, Daniel J . Sullivan, as a potential spoiler. This chicanery led to threats to invalidate the election from the Trump administration should Peltola win, but the courts have so far blocked that nonsense. The other Sullivan sits at 1.68 percent of the vote, behind a second Republican, Gerald Heikes, whose 2.26 percent has not earned the ire of the president.

Farmworker Democrats are ahead in Yakima Valley state House races: Legislative District 14 was redrawn by the courts to stop the suppression of the region’s Latino majority electorate, who ran two candidates this cycle from the farmworker movement to dethrone Republican legislators beholden to the latifundistas. As a carefully redrawn district, LD 14’s borders stretch into four separate rural counties, meaning this race may take a while to play out—but as of right now, Democratic challengers Chelsea Dimas and Ezequiel Morfin are both beating incumbent Republican legislators, by about 10 points.

Idiotic Montana conservative Democrat “Independent” Senate campaign fails: After Democrats in previously purple Montana who ran to the right lost every important statewide election two years in a row, followed by a US Senate seat, they had to come up with a plan: and they picked a really stupid one. Blame the Democratic party branding for looking too woke to the state’s chud electorate, and run a right-wing Democrat for Senate as an Independent instead to trick them. But there was someone party leaders forgot to ask: primary voters who elected a Democratic nominee who refused to bow to pressure from Blue Dog threats and party leaders to step down and clear the way for Seth Bodnar, the “Independent.” The result is a split vote on the left resulting in another Republican seat in the Senate in what otherwise should have been another blue wave victory. Had Montana Democrats simply run Bodnar as a Democrat, he would have won, as Sam Forstag did, winning one of Montana’s two Congressional seats for Democrats on a progressive affordability campaign endorsed by Bernard Sanders.

Tacoma LOVES their far-right sheriff who threatened the legislature: Voters in Pierce County had the opportunity to rid themselves of their “constitutional” sheriff this election, but appear to have decided not to. That means an ex-Seattle cop who doesn’t recognize the authority of the state legislature will still be big dog in the county that hosts the Pacific Northwest’s largest immigrant concentration camp. An amendment to the county charter would have changed the office of sheriff from an elected to an appointed position (as it was until 2006) but current results have it failing 33-66. That’s a big deficit to make up over this week’s count.

Things look bad for Democratic opponents of the Millionaires Tax: Not only did voters reject repealing it last night, but income tax reform’s highest profile Democrat is currently losing reelection. Eastside Rep. Amy Walen went into yesterday having already lost her primary to progressive challenger Jessica Forsythe by a handful of votes, and she’s behind again as of last night by 4 points. Microsoft spent a Yes,small fortune backing her up, so it’s one to watch for tax reform nerds.

Georgia is certainly on our minds. First, Sen. Jon Ossoff crushed MAGA’s Mike Collins (the former got 60 percent of the vote ). And Atlanta’s former mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms soundly defeated billionaire Republican Rick Jackson (he spent $200 million of his own cash on his campaign). And in case you didn’t know, Bottoms will become the US first Black woman governor .
Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan, despite (or because of) all the bullshit. We’ll give Seattle Rep. Pramila Jayapal the first word on this.

“Abdul was up against millions of dollars in dark money from Republican donors — and today Michigan voters sent a clear message that their state and their votes are not for sale. Abdul ran a strong campaign on Medicare For All, refused corporate PAC money, and stayed focused on working families from day one to Election Day.”

Jayapal recently told us that a big Democratic majority can help her pass legislation to block military aid to Israel, or at least make it contingent on human rights reforms. We imagine El-Sayed will be working closely on that.

Texas’ first Hispanic governor will be a rebuke to at least one homicidal white supremecist. Democrat Gina Hinojosa beat incumbent Gov. Gregg Abbott handily, on a platform for supporting public schools and lowering household costs .

El Paso won’t miss you, Gov. Gregg Abbott. Cedar covered the Walmart massacre in El Paso in 2019, when a white supremecist drove to Dallas to murder 23 people in the border city, part of a bid to start a race war. Abbott diagnosed the problem, as the Texas Tribune quoted him “In this case, we’re dealing with domestic terrorism. We’re dealing with a white supremacist. We’re dealing with racism.”

He failed to diagnose the cause. Abbott’s own racism, his own white supremecist ideology and embrace of Great Replacement Theory, mirrored that of the young man who authored the massacre. “If we’re going to DEFEND Texas, we’ll need to take matters into our own hands,” Abbott said in an Aug. 2, 2019 fundraising mailer, “In just six months (of illegal immigrant crossings), we’d add the population of Arlington.” For some, Abbott’s legacy is that he oversaw around 60 state executions in his three terms, killing around the same number of Hispanic people as that of the Walmart shooter. The shooter, meanwhile, managed to get life in prison.

The border is now blue, and has its first indigenous Governor, Laguna Pueblo tribal member Democrat Deb Haaland. New Mexico is more than 10 percent indigenous, the most native population in the US after Hawaii and Alaska. Haaland was born in the 1960s when tribal residents in New Mexico didn’t even have the right to vote (tribal addresses were considered outside the US). Now she’ll lead the state, and grapple with how to treat oil companies who are destroying the planet (and her legacy as Secretary of the Interior under Biden) and also funding the state’s education and childcare programs, Mother Jones reports .

LA could get its own Mamdani: The mayoral race between incumbent Karen Bass and DSA-backed City Councilmember Nithya Raman was nearly a dead heat on election night, but Raman has pulled narrowly ahead . Raman should get most of the late ballots, so this doesn’t bode well for Bass despite police unions and business groups funneling millions into PACs against Raman.

Billionaire-loving Californians cocked this one up: It is not looking good for the California ballot proposition that would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on people and trusts with over $1 billion in assets. Currently, 55.6 percent of voters rejected the measure and 44.4 percent approved. California is a majority vote-by-mail state these days, so later returns could skew left, but that’s a lot of ground to make up.
Let’s end AM with an immortal track by the father of techno , Detroit’s Juan Atkins. The genius died on Saturday after spending 64 years on this, our one and only dark star.

articles.title: Four Years Ago, Vito’s Beloved Stuffed Cougar Went Missing
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: During Thanksgiving weekend of 2022, Vito’s was deprived of a key part of its identity, a taxidermy cougar named Barbara.

Killed somewhere in Northern Canada some 20 years before the start of the present millennium, and purchased in 2010 by Vito’s owners , Greg Lundgren and Jeff Scott, the beast commanded the back room reserved for private events.

Whatever or whoever Barbara was in life, we can only imagine. For sure, she walked on snow, and she killed a bunch of animals, and she certainly saw the moon in a sky that was clear and cold, but didn’t think much of it. Cougars are not philosophical or poetic (that’s the business of bears). Then one day she unfortunately crossed paths with this world’s prime predator—a deadly, big-brained, bipedal primate—and was, with a bullet, dispatched into the next world (do cougars have souls?).

Eventually, the dead animal was gutted, tanned, preserved, and transformed into a sculpture that found its way to a bar and restaurant that had a long and rich history in Seattle. Here, in this tooth-and-claw-red room, the Cougar Room, Barbara nobly reposed on rocks and greenery as distant mountains and clouds rose phantasmagorically behind her. The gorgeous and campy scene, designed by Jennifer Zeyl and painted by Jason Puccinelli, defined the restaurant, if not Seattle, in that moment in time: the second decade of the century.

Some, like myself, do still think about her, and do have theories about who might have stolen the icon. For example, the same weekend Barbara vanished, the University of Washington Huskies soundly defeated Washington State University Cougars 51 to 33 in Pullman. Should this coincidence be ignored or explored? It’s not hard to picture fraternity brothers from either university doing this job as a flex or for revenge. Or maybe it was a millionaire collector who could not resist the opportunity of adding this priceless piece of Seattle history to their secret collection. Barbara is now for their eyes alone.

Her owners offered $1,000 for her return, no questions asked, or $2,000 for information that led to the arrest of the thief or thieves. (Barbara was valued at $15,000.) But the police never made any arrests.

There was a rumor that someone who broke into Vito’s after the fire stole a check and attempted to cash it in their very own bank account. Obviously not a very bright person. Obviously a great lead. But when reached by text, Lundgren tells me there were “no charges” on the check writer. Evidently, the SPD did not think much of this case or its subject, Barbara.

“I miss Vito’s in the fall especially,” says Lundgren. The same goes with me. I miss walking into the dark joint from the cold or rain or falling leaves. I miss the mirrors in the vestibule, the large meatballs during happy hour, the chill wine list, the jazz singers and players performing standards, the underworld-like atmosphere, and, of course, the cougar. Many people still miss the cougar. Wherever you are, Barbara, you’re still in our thoughts.

articles.title: Levitating Together
articles.author: Audrey Vann
paras: When XOË (pronounced X-O-E) began making music together a year and a half ago, they had no preconceived notions about what influences might come to the surface. “I feel like it’s only been since the end of last year that we’ve really found our sound,” the band’s keyboardist, Max Irvine, tells me. “And even then, we’re still figuring it out in real time with the audience.” At this point in time, XOË sound like what would happen if Erykah Badu fronted a Paisley Underground band. Or if Jill Scott were backed by the Bad Seeds. Or if D’Angelo played a set at the Roadhouse in Twin Peaks . Or if Sault merged with Portishead—I could go on like this forever, but no hypothetical comparison can fully encapsulate the sound of XOË.

The band came together organically, when drummer Saba Samakar, a session musician in Seattle for over a decade, invited a few people over to his studio to jam. One of them was Adrian Michael, a skilled drummer, guitarist, and bassist, whom he’d met kickboxing at his gym. Another was Irvine, a trained jazz pianist and self-taught guitarist who’d been studying music since he was 4. On this particular day, Zoë Duarte stopped by the studio to drop off a roommate’s dog whom she was walking, and Samakar asked if she wablunted to join. “She was very quiet that day,” Samakar recalls. “Yeah, I don’t think I said shit!” Duarte says with a laugh. “There were just all these dudes I didn’t know… I was so nervous. At that time, I hadn’t sung in front of many people.”

From the moment we sat down for an interview, the band conveyed their nervousness. “Audrey, we are a little scared,” Samakar tells me, half joking. At first, I don’t buy it. XOË caught my attention at Den Fest—the annual showcase for Den Tapes—due to their hard-to-pin-down sound and commanding onstage presence. I found myself completely enchanted by Duarte, whose demeanor and voice were something in between To Bring You My Love –era PJ Harvey and Frank -era Amy Winehouse. She hypnotizes onlookers with her voice, yet floats around the stage, Lynchian-style, mysteriously looking at the floor. When a song ends, she looks up shyly and flashes a bright, dimpled smile. Despite this angelic onstage presence, Duarte tells me that she suffers from deep stage fright. “I think it’s actually gotten worse the more I play,” she says. “Every show, I’m like, ‘Let’s get out of here!’”

Duarte has always been a singer. “I just am drawn to it,” she tells me. “It’s what makes me the happiest.” In fourth grade, she recorded a tape of herself singing Aretha Franklin’s “Respect” for a school project. In high school, she joined the school choir and jazz ensemble, but didn’t find it fulfilling. She daydreamed about being in a band, but considered it ​​unattainable. “I thought nobody was gonna want to fucking collaborate with me,” she recalls. “I’m too nervous!” Eventually, she started singing over leased beats in her bedroom and writing her own songs, which would later evolve into XOË’s first EP, XOËP . “It’s actually a crazy dream to be in this band,” says Duarte. “When I think about what we’ve done, I’m just like, holy shit! It’s a fucking dream. The dream’s happening.”

“Our songwriting process is highly collaborative,” says Samakar, explaining that he’ll often bring what he thinks is a finished song to band practice, only to see it change and evolve through the minds of his bandmates, or, as he describes, “they’ll freak it.” Duarte, who writes the lyrics, cites ’80s avant-pop artist Anna Domino (who famously synth-ified Aretha Franklin’s “Land of My Dreams”) as key inspiration, along with Erykah Badu, the Cure, and Boy Harsher. She will bring simple guitar chords and lyrics to rehearsals and describe through words, noises, or even pictures what she wants it to sound like. “We play around until Zoë goes, ‘OH YEAH!’—that’s when I know I’ve done something right,” Irvine explains. Duarte points to her bandmates: “These guys are so fucking talented. They can make a song into this beautiful, complete thing.”

XOË thrive on polarities: They are experimental and heavy, yet easy and warm. “Someone once called us ‘doom soul,’ and we like that,” Irvine says. The band never had a proper conversation about what they wanted to sound like, and they resist an explicit genre label.

However, Samakar admits that, whether it’s the intent or not, their individual musical inspirations will make their way into the room like friendly ghosts. Among the inspirations mentioned were Bill Evans, Donny Hathaway, Carole King, MonoNeon, the Roots, and Animals as Leaders, along with ’90s grunge and classic video game soundtracks.

The boys all agree that their main goal is to make Duarte shine. “She has such an amazing voice,” says Irvine. “But all of us shine!” offers Duarte. “That’s the only way it works. Each person must passionately feel their instrument and really give it everything. We always talk about putting it all in, no matter what.” Samakar interjects: “You can say it… Put your pussy into it!”

Given that XOË is a relatively new project with just two EPs out, most of the gigs they’re booking are opening sets at modest venues. “I don’t care if I’m playing to two people or 50 people,” Irvine says. “Just having people allow us to get onstage and just show our whole ass—you know, like, artistically—it’s such a privilege to me.” The band isn’t fueled by arbitrary measures of success, but rather their earnest passion, genuine friendship, and love of playing. “This is one of the few groups that I’m onstage, I can mess up, and we all just laugh,” Michael tells me.

“We’re all really fucking passionate about what we play and how we play it,” says Duarte. “When we play, we are all fucking levitating together because—it’s cheesy—but this is why we’re here. This is what gets us up. This is the one thing that makes us feel ourselves.”

articles.title: What to Do If You See ICE
articles.author: Stranger Staff
paras: Print, fold, and keep this ’zine on hand so you know how and where to report an ICE sighting. You can submit photos and video, and search for ICE license plate information, anytime at ICEout.org. The Washington Immigration Solidarity Network announced staff layoffs in October, and its Deportation Defense Hotline is only monitored Monday–Friday, 7 a.m. to 2 p.m.

FILM IT Use your phone to record everything. If you are in public, or on your own property, you have a right to film. Note the time, location, the number of agents, what they’re wearing, their equipment and/or weapons, and license plate numbers.
OFFER TO HELP If ICE is detaining someone, ask the person(s) being detained for their name, and if they have an emergency contact you can reach out to.

ASK QUESTIONS Telling the agents, “I’m just observing, I will not interfere,” can de-escalate the situation. Ask the officers what agency they’re with, why they’re detaining the person, and where they’re taking them.
GATHER WITNESSES Exchange contact information with anyone else at the scene. They may have more videos, prior contact with the detainee, or know how to contact their friends or family.

KNOW YOUR AGENCIES Avoid spreading misinformation. Was it really ICE? Virtually all sectors of federal law enforcement have participated in ICE raids, but it’s important to confirm that what you witnessed was, in fact, an ICE arrest or raid. By state law, Seattle police cannot collaborate with ICE.
Washington Immigrant Solidarity Network (WAISN) 1-844-724-3737 Mon-Fri 7 am-2 pm
On the Eastside: Eastside for All eastsideforall.org (425) 361-0808

If your rights have been violated, file a complaint with the Washington State Office of the Attorney General at atg.wa.gov . For immigration help, contact the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project at NWIRP.org or Legal Immigration Services of Olympia at lisowa.org .

ICE ACTIVITY SURGED THIS SUMMER According to the Deportation Data Project, ICE arrested about 1,400 people in Washington across June and July (up from about 230 in February). While witnesses and bystanders have been invaluable in documenting ICE’s tactics and potential rights violations, it isn’t for everyone. People have been injured and killed when interacting with ICE agents. Recording and reporting ICE activity is just one way to help.

articles.title: Where to Scream
articles.author: Megan Seling
paras: Solidarity Day with Seattle Democratic Socialists of America Nov 14 La Resistencia, which started in 2014 to “end immigrant detention and deportations in Washington,” regularly hosts vigils outside the detention center and monitors deportation flights out of the King County International Airport. On November 14, they’ll be joined by members of the Seattle Democratic Socialists of America. They also collect donations via PayPal ( @laresistencia ) and Venmo ( @LaResistenciaNW ) to help detainees buy food and supplies from the commissary. Keep an eye on their socials for more ways to help. ( Northwest Detention Center, Tacoma, 1–3 pm )

Scream Club Seattle Nov 15 Here is, quite literally, where you can scream if you need to unleash all your rage, anxiety, and frustration on a primal level. Scream Club Seattle meets twice monthly—on the first Sunday at Lincoln Park and the third Sunday at Golden Gardens—and everyone is invited to join in the collective catharsis.

The club’s founder, Amber Walcker, started the Seattle chapter last summer, after seeing the idea take off in Chicago. Now anywhere from five to 45 people have joined her at the water’s edge to unleash their pent-up emotions. She says Scream Club is very different than screaming alone in your car or into a pillow.

“Screaming over the water, you’re actually projecting, and you’re giving the energy out of your body and giving it space to go to, but it’s also [about] the reaction right after,” says Walcker. “When you have 10, 15, 20 people screaming around you, when that scream stops, you can hear the water so differently. Your body feels more present, and your mind is able to take things in because you just had this huge endorphin rush. Being able to hear the waves, it’s very calming after a scream.”

People at Scream Club scream for all kinds of reasons. “It’s really about an emotional release, whether that’s for joy, for anger, grief, whatever. Everyone [screams] however they feel is meaningful to them.” And the event is quick, just a few minutes, and it includes three guided screams. The first is kind of a warm-up; it’s meant to settle the butterflies and help people get over the awkwardness of screaming in public. By the third scream, “that’s really when that release comes,” says Walcker.

Some people laugh, some people cry, some people stick around afterward to visit, and others scream and leave without saying a word. There are no rules at Scream Club. “I say, ‘Hey, if you feel like you need to drop to your knees or become almost like an animal, get on all fours and scream from your soul, however it feels right to you, just know you are in a safe space where everyone’s here to do the same exact thing, so feel zero judgment.’” The next Scream Club is November 15 at 11:30 a.m. at Golden Gardens. They post all their events on Instagram at @screamclubsea . SEE YOU THERE!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

Riff Raff League Nov 15 and 29 Every other Sunday, Seattle’s most punk-rock art shop, Push/Pull, hosts free Riff Raff League meetings where folks can talk about political action and mutual aid while making zines, posters, buttons, and whistle kits for their neighbors. While you’re there, grab a free ABOLISH ICE poster and sign up for one of their monthly zine-making workshops! Masks are required. RSVPs are appreciated, but they will not turn anyone away. ( Push/Pull, 7:15–8:15 pm )

articles.title: REVIEW | That Turquoise Building Near Rainier Beach Station? It's a Polynesian Deli
paras: If you're like me, you've passed the turquoise-tinged building of the Vegetable Bin near the Rainier Beach light rail station countless times. The unmissable roof has long sloped sides evoking a building from somewhere on the other side of the world. There are a few advertisements for products on the windows and two empty display cases with "Vegetable Bin" and "Polynesian Deli" written across the top.
Those who visit this convenience store often seek more than convenience — they want a taste of home.

Tae Kim's uncle started the Vegetable Bin back in the '90s. The store sold only produce until a customer, a Samoan pastor, suggested adding Polynesian food. Kim's uncle traveled to Samoa with the pastor and learned to cook the cuisine so he could replicate it back home at the store. Photos of the trip are framed and hang on the back wall behind the deli counter.
Kim explained that back then, it was much harder to get these Polynesian staples, like huge quantities of canned corned beef and coconut milk, which can still be difficult to find at that scale.

These days, the Vegetable Bin menu is fairly simple: boiled and baked taro, boiled green banana, turkey tails, pork sausage, corned beef, lamb flaps, palusami (coconut cream and onion in steamed taro leaves), and Spam musubi.
The deli section sits in the back of the store. It has a couple of tables and chairs set up in front of the hot food counter.

During my visit, as I sat with my spread of dishes, two Samoan men sat at the table next to me. They opened their boxes of turkey tail, taro, and corned beef. From the store, they bought Hawaiian Sun sodas and canned corned beef. A little lost about how best to eat my own food, I struck up a conversation. They explained that you can eat the taro as a starch, like rice or bread, and mix the canned corned beef into the palusami.

It would be easy to walk in, glance at the dishes warming behind the glass counter, and wonder what all the fuss is about. Boiled banana doesn't exactly sound like the most interesting thing. And who knew that turkey tail was something anyone ate? (The answer to that can be traced back to Western influence.)

Yet the turkey tail is fatty and cooked in a teriyaki sauce that makes it pretty irresistible. I knew the least about the palusami. But I was pleasantly surprised by just how creamy and flavorful the coconut milk was inside the taro leaves. I learned that you eat the leaves, which, when cooked, soften like spinach. They have a floral fragrance to them and a mild nutty flavor, which pairs perfectly with the saltier coconut cream and onion mixture.

I also got a Spam musubi, which, as expected, I found satisfactory. There's nothing spectacular about how it was prepared, but that is the beauty of such a simple dish — it doesn't need much to be good.

Washington state has the third-largest Pacific Islander population in the U.S., according to the Washington State Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs . The Vegetable Bin caters to the community with its hot food counter and inventory of essentials, chips and other snacks from the South Pacific region, and frozen items like octopus and parrotfish.
The store has one aisle dedicated to canned foods like mackerel, Spam, and corned beef — not exactly "traditional" Polynesian food.

Canned foods were introduced to the Pacific Islands by U.S. and European colonizers in the late 19th century, according to ABC Pacific . These canned foods became prized possessions because of their long shelf life, their taste, and the fact that they were difficult to obtain. During the two world wars, these items were rationed to locals, making them a staple in their everyday diets.

As Islanders moved their diets away from traditional foods like taro, fruit, and fish and consumed more processed foods , their health decreased dramatically. In 2016, NPR reported that the Samoan islands had among the world's highest rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes.

The hot food section of the store used to be bigger, with a rotating menu including dishes like manapua (a steamed bun full of meat), octopus in coconut, and whole fried fish. But Kim says that due to a slowdown in customers, the shop narrowed its menu to just the favorites. He suspects that part of it is due to people from the community trying to watch their health.

While the food wasn't something I would find myself craving on any given day, I can understand why the Vegetable Bin is important to so many people. Eating classic dishes like turkey tail and taro may not conjure any memories or feelings for me, but it does for the Polynesian customers who are looking for the taste of something familiar.

Anyone who has traveled or lived somewhere else can understand the feeling. The things that we took for granted become some of the things that we miss most when we can't have them. It's not the best-looking or even necessarily the best-tasting food that we miss — it's the food our parents made for us that becomes synonymous with home.
That's the magic of what the Vegetable Bin offers.

articles.title: A look into how elections are certified in Washington
articles.author: Jaelynn Grisso
paras: Election day may be over, but the counting has just begun. The next month will include state and county election officials reviewing the ballot counts and certifying the results.
The process of certifying an election largely starts with the county, Washington’s Director of Elections Stuart Holmes said.

“Looking back at the 2004 governor's election, there was a lot of variation across the state,” he said. “Since that point in time, we've worked really closely as a state to ensure that there's consistency and standards for how different election processes must be done in the state of Washington.”
Local election offices use tabulation machines to count ballots, then state and local officials work together on what’s called election reconciliation.
“What that really means is we're accounting for every ballot that's been issued, and every ballot has been received by every county in the state of Washington,” Holmes said.

They have 21 days for reconciliation before submitting the findings to the county’s canvassing board, which then reviews the results. Once accepted, counties submit the results to the Secretary of State’s office. The agency then has nine days to certify multi-county races and statewide ballot measures.
The office requires tabulation machines to be tested before and after an election and only allows machines that cannot transmit wirelessly in any way.

“When we're talking about voting machines, there's a lot of concern about the accuracy of the voting machines and potentially, you know, a distrust with them in the outcomes,” Holmes said. “As election officials, we don't trust them either. That's why we do pre-election audits. We do post-election audits. We check them every, every possible way to confirm that they haven't been tampered with.”
They also work to detect fraud in voting, and one way they do that is by cross referencing the names of voters with lists from other states to catch anyone who may have voted in multiple states.
Holmes said the rate of fraud in the state is so low, it’s hard to measure.

“There are millions and millions of ballots that are cast and a very small amount of fraud. These small amounts still need to be treated seriously and investigated, but the fact remains that it's a very, very rare occurrence,” Holmes said.

articles.title: Why tradwives are fleeing the movement: ‘I can’t undo my past – but I can warn other women’
articles.author: Lucy Knight
paras: In recent years, some of the most vocal tradwives have left their husbands, renounced their religious faith and promoted financial independence. What is behind this sudden and seismic shift?

When Bernadine Bluntly posted a video earlier this year renouncing the tradwife movement she had championed, it caused shockwaves through the “alt-right” social media world. Previously, posts of her and her six children had flooded feeds as the Maga movement gained ground. She was one of the defiantly anti-feminist influencers who promoted a return to patriarchal gender roles, pronatalist ideals and fundamentalist Christian values – particularly around the sanctity of marriage. Bluntly, whose real surname is Barber, had, in the past, sold T-shirts reading “RIP Feminism”, supported Brett Kavanaugh’s nomination to the supreme court and developed a course, Simply Smitten, to help young women attract husbands who were “traditional masculine men”.

Then, last year, she left her husband. Her divorce was finalised this year. In the proceedings, she got a restraining order against her ex, whom she said was abusive (he denies this). In April, the 36-year-old posted a video titled: “ What I got wrong about the trad movement ”, in which she said that, while she is still a Christian and believes in the differences between men and women: “I no longer believe in extreme gender roles, especially when they’re wrapped in spiritual language and used to justify control, silence or harm.” She said that the tradwife movement, one she initially thought was about a “return to strong family values”, has “become indistinguishable from the current wave of the red-pill manosphere”. She concluded: “If my past content contributed to that, I am so genuinely sorry.”

articles.title: NASA’s Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failed – here’s why it’s so hard to boost a satellite
articles.author:
<name>Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba, Ph.D. Candidate in Aerospace Engineering, University of Florida</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/wanjiku-chebet-kanjumba-2685452"/>
paras: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth. NASA ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady. The telescope reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4 above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent observing powerful cosmic explosions .

Swift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026. LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, reentered Earth’s atmosphere in September . The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first.
As a Ph.D. candidate in aerospace engineering , I know that rescuing satellites is hard . I research how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably.

Swift’s loss points to a new hazard for the young industry that repairs, refuels and moves spacecraft around in orbit. If something goes wrong, the spacecraft doing the rescuing can become another problem.

The plan was for LINK to approach Swift, grab it with one of its three robotic arms and fire its thrusters to push the telescope back up to about 373 miles (600 kilometers) above Earth’s surface, where it could keep observing for years.

In late July, LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels , which are heavy wheels inside a spacecraft that help it turn without using fuel. That loss, combined with problems with its propulsion system, sent the spacecraft into an uncontrolled spin.
Without working wheels, a spacecraft steers with its thrusters instead, and every burn spends propellant.

Engineers eventually slowed LINK’s rotation by firing its thrusters against the spin . NASA reported in August that they had cut its spin from about nine degrees per second to roughly one and a half degrees per second.

NASA and Katalyst Space, LINK’s builder, called off the capture and boost later in August . The team still flew LINK within 7.5 to 9 miles (12 to 15 kilometers) of Swift, where it deployed LINK’s three robotic arms and tested its electric thrusters. It never got close enough to grab the telescope.

A servicing spacecraft, like LINK, launches with a finite supply of propellant. Engineers split that fuel supply among the mission’s jobs, from reaching the target and approaching it safely to capturing it and moving it to a new orbit. They also pack some extra fuel in case of surprises.
Think of a tow truck that burns most of its gas getting itself out of a ditch. Even if it reaches a broken-down car, it may not have enough fuel left to tow it home.

That scenario is close to what happened to LINK. Even after engineers brought its spin under control, Katalyst said the spacecraft no longer had enough propellant to capture Swift and raise its orbit safely.

A fuel budget that covers only the planned steps leaves nothing for recovering from a fault. But every extra pound of propellant also makes a spacecraft heavier, and heavier spacecraft cost more to launch and take more fuel to move.

Starting in 2024, solar activity swelled Earth’s upper atmosphere, and the extra drag pulled Swift down faster than expected. Once NASA saw how quickly Swift was falling, the agency had to move fast to try to save the observatory. Space missions typically take years to develop and launch, but in this case, a slow, conventional development program risked arriving too late.
NASA awarded Katalyst a US$30 million contract in September 2025. The company had less than a year to design, build, test and launch LINK . LINK launched on July 3, 2026.

Speed comes with trade-offs. In engineering, a compressed schedule can leave less time for repeated testing, building spare hardware and planning recovery options. Public reports do not say whether that trade-off played any part in LINK’s faults.

NASA has said that even though LINK didn’t succeed, the effort gave the agency experience in quickly building, launching and operating a servicing spacecraft. Engineers also showed they could upload new control software to steady a damaged servicing spacecraft with the hardware it had left. And LINK tested its arms and fired all three thrusters at once in orbit.

While Swift was the most pressing case for a boost mission, it’s not the only one. NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope could one day use a similar boost, and news reports suggested it would have been next in line had this mission worked.

Future missions are pursuing two complementary approaches for rescuing satellites. Astroscale’s ELSA-M is built to capture satellites that carry a docking plate installed before launch, which would make it easier for a rescuer to snag and boost them if the satellite eventually got into trouble. The European Space Agency’s ClearSpace-1 is planned for 2029 and aims to capture the Proba-1 satellite, which doesn’t have a docking plate or anything to help ClearSpace-1 capture it, and remove it from orbit.

LINK’s mission showed that a rescue takes more than a robotic arm and enough thrust to reach a target. It also takes a servicer spacecraft that can stay stable, recover from its own faults and keep enough propellant reserved to finish the job. In Swift’s case, the rescuer fell short before the rescue could begin.

articles.title: Pennsylvania Democrats now have power to push forward on election reform, marijuana legalization and minimum wage increases
articles.author:
<name>Daniel J. Mallinson, Associate Professor of Public Policy and Administration, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/daniel-j-mallinson-572958"/>
paras: The 2026 midterm elections changed the balance of power in Washington, D.C. It also proved to be a pivotal election in Pennsylvania.

Gov. Josh Shapiro handily defeated Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer. Not only that, it looks like Democrats will expand their majority in the state House and have flipped the state Senate , earning a 26-24 majority.
That gives Shapiro the coveted party trifecta – single party control of both the governor’s office and the General Assembly.
Given the pent-up demand among Democrats who have not fully controlled Harrisburg for over 30 years , the excitement is palpable among Pennsylvania Democrats.

I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in Pennsylvania state politics . Now that the political fault lines are clear for the next two years in Pennsylvania’s state government, it is worth considering what Democrats may do with their newfound power.
For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House has been sending the Republican-controlled Senate.
Election reform has been a perennial priority in Pennsylvania since the passage of Act 77 of 2019 and the 2020 election.

Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting where voters could vote all at once for a single party, which was a bipartisan compromise but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results. No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail.

Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties in Pennsylvania to use ballot drop boxes , maintain no-excuse mail-in voting , set clear rules for ballot curing where voters are able to correct issues with their submitted mail ballots instead of having them invalidated, institute precanvassing to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allow independents to vote in open primary elections .
Democrats may now be able to pass all of these without having to compromise with Republican demands for stricter voter ID requirements.

Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House passed a legalization bill in 2025 . Democrats had said that they will legalize recreational marijuana if they took the Senate in 2026. But important details of legalization remain to be worked out, even with Democratic control.
Democrats have sponsored divergent bills on whether sales should be through private dispensaries or state stores , similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania.

Social equity measures meant to repair some of the harms of the war on drugs on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage. These include things such as expungements of past convictions, setting aside licenses for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues.

Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details. But a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania makes it even more likely that the commonwealth will be among the next states where adult-use recreational marijuana is legal.

The House has passed several measures to regulate artificial intelligence and the data center build-out in the commonwealth. This includes a measure that would require warnings on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target energy costs , water use , local government authority and implementing and the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development plan.

These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda. Additionally, criticism over the AI-generated ads fielded by the Garrity campaign , which are regulated in other states , may add this issue to the state’s AI policy agenda.

Given that this election was likely heavily influenced by voters’ concerns about affordability , Democrats will need to show progress on bringing down prices where they can. The Democrats’ Affordability Action Plan includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding.

Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7.25 minimum hourly wage over time. The bill passed by the House in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it also had been passed by the Senate. This is important in Philadelphia, given that state law prohibits the city from setting its own minimum wage. The legislation will have to be introduced and passed again by the new General Assembly.

Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges decision by the U.S. Supreme Court, but the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent.

Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House tried to change in 2026 to “two individuals.” Democrats are very likely to pick this back up and may even attempt a more durable, but also more procedurally difficult , constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights.

Pennsylvania also does not include LGBTQ individuals in its nondiscrimination protections. The Democrats in the House passed a bill that would add sexual orientation and gender identity to the state’s Human Relations Act in 2026, but it also died in the Senate. Democrats are likely to pick this up again in 2027.
Ultimately, Democrats will not be able to do everything. They will need to decide what to prioritize and what to leave behind.
Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania , or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack .

articles.title: Midterms are bad for incumbents – and even worse when energy prices are high
articles.author:
<name>Michael A. Mische, Associate Professor of the Practice of Management and Organization, Marshall School of Business, University of Southern California</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/michael-a-mische-2774325"/>
paras: As Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “ It’s the economy, stupid .” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy , making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise.
Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C.

Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think , because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers , with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz , which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on.
When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food , follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally .

Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection . For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record .
Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections.

Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month , and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32% .
When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3% , and gas prices were still high .
Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “ Whip Inflation Now ,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats.
“WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter.
In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly . Inflation hit 9% in 1978 .

In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats . Inflation continued to climb , and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976 . Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan.

Reagan implemented “ Reaganomics ” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum . By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut , lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs .
In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate.

Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate.

In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22% . In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate .

Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40% . Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups.
And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon .
Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies.

Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon .

But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord , under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source.
In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1% , a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon ; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today.

The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots.

During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5% , U.S. oil production rose 3.3% , from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon .

On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted , though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels .

Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026.
As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices , as well as an unpopular war .

It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future , they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties.

articles.title: How a French philosopher’s warnings about speed and power describe today’s AI race
articles.author:
<name>Shahnaz Bashir, Ph.D. Candidate in Communication, UMass Amherst</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/shahnaz-bashir-2765152"/>
paras: With the race to build artificial intelligence systems smarter than any human has come a boom in “accidents.” In a safety test run by the company Anthropic , its own AI agent blackmailed an engineer to avoid being shut down. Criminals have used AI agents for data-extortion campaigns and to hack government agencies , banks and technology companies. In other tests, models have escaped from test environments into real organizational systems .

Several researchers who resigned from leading AI companies in 2026 have accused their employers of not taking the dangers seriously enough . In September, Bill Gates told “Meet the Press” that AI is “ powerful enough to drive events that can cause a billion deaths .”

Paul Virilio, a French philosopher, spent his career analyzing the relationships between technology, speed and power . He died in 2018 , well before generative AI and the fears about it reached their present pitch. But I doubt much would have surprised him.

As a researcher who studies AI-generated media and how people make sense of it, I find that three of Virilio’s ideas explain today’s AI moment better than anything written since. He argued that every new technology brings a new kind of accident into the world ; that speed takes away our time to think ; and that globally connected systems can fail everywhere at once.

Virilio was born in Paris in 1932. When World War II began, his family moved to Nantes, a port city near the Atlantic. During the Nazi occupation of France, Germany began building the Atlantic Wall , a series of defensive fortifications stretching along the coast from Spain to Norway.

But in September 1943, when he was 11, Virilio saw what the wall could not keep out. American bombers aiming for Nantes’ port hit the city center instead , killing about 1,400 people and destroying more than 700 buildings in two raids.
“War was my university,” he told an interviewer . “Everything has proceeded from there.”

As a young man, Virilio spent years photographing the abandoned bunkers of the Atlantic Wall. The lesson he drew from them was about speed: The Germans had built a massive military fortification, yet the Allies had gone over and around it; the wall barely slowed them.
Walls were a technology of space, and the bombers were a technology of speed – inspiring his philosophical approach to understanding the world.
As an adult, Virilio studied many more examples of technological failures, such as the Chernobyl power plant meltdown of 1986, the worst nuclear accident in history.

In his 2005 book “ The Original Accident ,” Virilio summed up his main idea in a simple sentence: “To invent the sailing ship or steamer is to invent the shipwreck.” The train invents derailment; the airplane, the crash; the nuclear plant, the meltdown. Every invention, not just dangerous ones, carries a specific kind of failure that did not exist before it.

In Virilio’s telling, the “accident” is not the result of bad luck added afterward. It is born at the moment of invention, even if the inventor cannot see it, because the invention will be used in ways they never imagined.

Virilio did not think such accidents could be avoided. But by carefully watching, he believed, people could contain failure and prevent catastrophe. He argued that societies tend to treat each disaster as a one-off, grieve it on television, and forget it, so that the next technology’s accident arrives as a surprise.

In 2002, he staged a Paris exhibition as a trial run for his plan to build a “Museum of Accidents.” Collecting information about shipwrecks, plane crashes, industrial disasters and financial crashes side by side, he argued, would show the pattern: that every invention has its failure and that failure can be anticipated .
AI has invented not one accident but several . Tech companies’ own incident reports form a sort of “museum” – but not an objective one.
Virilio’s second key idea came from the Cold War. In 1977, he published “ Speed and Politics ,” written in a world where nuclear missiles could cross the planet in minutes.

He named the idea “dromology,” derived from the Greek word for a racecourse: “dromos .” Every age runs at the pace of its fastest machine, Virilio wrote, and whatever cannot keep up – including law, deliberation and conscience – drops out of the picture. There is “no democracy, only dromocracy”: the rule of the fastest.

AI can squeeze months of work into hours. In September 2026, Open AI announced that 10,000 of its AI agents had produced a proof of a math problem that had stood for a century – a problem two human mathematicians had spent a year trying to solve .

Virilio’s deepest fear about speed was not that people would fall behind machines, but that they would be absent from decision-making. Even when people attempt to stay in the loop, AI agents execute so quickly that human workers often fail to spot problems or malicious requests .
Virilio’s third idea is the “integral accident”: a failure that, because the same technology runs everywhere, happens everywhere at once .

During the 1990s, Virilio watched how satellite television, the internet and electronic markets let an event anywhere, such as a financial crash, be felt everywhere. He later predicted that in a networked world, integral accidents, not war, would be “ the continuation of politics by other means .”
AI has intensified how tightly connected the world is. It’s being used to help balance power grids , manage ships and harbors , and write hospital patient records .

Consider Anthropic’s Claude Mythos model, which finds security flaws in banking software faster than banks can fix them. Many financial institutions use the same software, so a criminal with such a model could break into multiple banks at the same time.

Virilio wrote that a society that lives only in the present makes accidents more likely . A society too busy to keep records of its past, or to think ahead, cannot learn from its failures and so repeats them.
I’d argue that that sentence points to three things worth keeping in mind.
The first is the record, kept by someone independent. Documents analyzing AI accidents should not be left only in the hands of the companies whose failures they document.
The second is the pause. Regulators, researchers and companies need the time and the authority to deliberate – and to halt a system, if needed, before it is released.

The third is skill. A skill is the present result of past practice. The more work people hand to AI because it is faster, the more they need to keep the ability to do that work themselves: to write the first draft, to check the sum by hand. These are the habits that let people verify what AI produces .

Virilio’s lesson is not to smash the machines, but to keep a hand on the lever – improving the chances that the accident, when it comes, can be seen, understood and reversed. Speed does not take the controls away, but it makes it harder for people to keep hold.

articles.title: Why a company donating $20,000 a month counts for more than $240,000 once a year in the eyes of customers
articles.author:
<name>Yanyi Leng, Assistant Professor of Marketing, Colorado State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/yanyi-leng-2772868"/>
paras: People tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount.

This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people . The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team.
Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts.

Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies.

To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal , a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank.

We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad.

Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke , a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000.

Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same.

Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes.

U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place.

Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026.

Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations . This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over.

Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off.
We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty.

It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense.

Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder , a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves.
The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work.

articles.title: A Feejee Mermaid on display in Colorado may shock and intrigue – but it’s no longer considered a ‘missing link’ on the evolutionary tree
articles.author:
<name>Jack Daly, Lecturer in Writing and Rhetoric, University of Colorado Boulder</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jack-daly-2772650"/>
paras: Mermaids have inhabited world folklore and mythology for centuries. Ancient Babylonians worshipped Oannes , a human-fish hybrid; sirens populated Greek mythology ; and fairy tales such as “ The Little Mermaid ” have made this figure a pop culture icon.

During the 1800s, American showman P.T. Barnum brought the Feejee Mermaid to the American public. Presented at the American Museum, run by Barnum in Manhattan from 1841 to 1865 , as “ The Greatest Curiosity in the World ” and said to have originated in the “Feejee Islands,” the creature inspired debates about science and evolution. Some people believed it was a missing link in the evolutionary chain between aquatic and terrestrial life.

I recently viewed a Feejee Mermaid replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science as part of the “ Mythic Creatures: Dragons, Unicorns and Mermaids” temporary exhibit . As a folklorist , I’m intrigued by how this mermaid subverted Americans’ expectations that mermaids are alluring and how it sparked an interplay between science and myth.

A Feejee Mermaid is a type of traditional art form that originated in Japan and the East Indies more than 400 years ago. It came to Americans in 1842, when Barnum claimed to display a “specimen” at the American Museum in New York City.

In the Japanese version, the lower half was a fish attached to an upper half of a monkey or made of papier-mâché. Barnum’s was a mixture of a monkey and a fish, but the replica on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science has a papier-mâché upper half. Feejee Mermaids were often preserved by being coated in clay .

Mammalian-fish hybrid creatures have a role in Japanese folklore through the ningyo , which are a mermaidlike yokai, a supernatural being thought to have the power to either curse or grant eternal life. Unlike Western mermaids, ningyo were grotesque.

The Feejee Mermaid that became part of Barnum’s exhibition was created by a Japanese fisherman in the early 19th century. He claimed to have caught the specimen and said it prophesied a sterility epidemic. The only cure for the townsfolk, the fisherman said, came through owning a picture of the mermaid.
Samuel Barrett Eades, an American sailor, purchased the Feejee Mermaid and willed it to his son, who then sold it to Moses Kimball , a curator at the Boston Museum, in 1842.
In his autobiography, Barnum details the scheme he devised after Kimball showed him the Feejee Mermaid.

Barnum sent letters to newspapers, describing how a “Dr. Griffin,” who was really his hoaxing accomplice Levi Lyman, was in possession of the mermaid skeleton. He further spread the word by distributing thousands of pamphlets throughout New York City that detailed when the mermaid would be on display and highlighted the seductive nature of mermaids.
However, when the public arrived at the American Museum, much to their surprise, they found Barnum’s grotesque version.

Barnum himself described it as “an ugly dried-up, black-looking diminutive specimen, about three feet long. Its mouth was open, its tail turned over and its arms thrown up, giving it the appearance of having died in great agony.”

The Feejee Mermaid on display at the Denver Museum of Nature and Science, and owned by the Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, may or may not be the one shown by Barnum. The museum says it is a replica.

The original was likely destroyed or disfigured in a fire at Barnum’s museum or the Boston Museum. The object on display looks quite different compared to original descriptions of the Feejee Mermaid. As originally shown, it was said to be much more monkeylike, and artistic renderings of it from the period matched Barnum’s descriptions.

Feejee Mermaids, as displayed in America, are characteristic of a “ sideshow gaff ” that interested Victorian audiences due to debates about evolution and science. In fact, 18th-century Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus had left space for mermaids in the evolutionary tree . The Feejee Mermaid, as it blended human and animal characteristics, folklore and science, spectacle and empiricism, displays how a monstrous hoax inspired fierce intellectual debates in 19th-century America.
