articles.title: Sara Nelson Leads Dark Money Attacks on Jenks, Seeking to Keep Centrists' Grip on Seattle Council
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: As Election Day arrives, much holds in the balance. Nationally, attention will be on whether polling that hints at a national blue wave will allow Democrats to seize control of both chambers of Congress will come to pass and provide a check on President Donald Trump's power and erratic decision making.

Locally, a special election in Seattle Council District 5 presents an opportunity for the progressive coalition to gain a seat and momentum heading into the 2027 election when all seven district seats will be on the ballot. Progressive standard-bearer Nilu Jenks has the advantage based on primary results , when she won 54% of the vote. The Urbanist Elections Committee (on which I serve) endorsed Jenks .
However, centrist donors are spending aggressively to prop up former bank chair Julie Kang in hopes of closing the gap. They're using a familiar formula , seeking to paint Jenks as soft on crime.

In their haste, a pro-Kang political action committee (PAC) called North Seattle Neighbors potentially broke election laws to rush attack ads out the door, and the Jenks campaign is calling on the PAC to fully disclose its donors and has appealed to the Seattle Ethics and Elections Commission seeking a cease-and-desist order barring it from "any further political advertising until it files every overdue report and discloses all its contributors and the true sources of its money."
John Wyble, a spokesperson for the Jenks campaign, argued this dark money-fueled attack ads has no place in Seattle politics.

"This is how Republican super PACs operate in swing states: scary pictures, old quotes, and money nobody can trace. It has no place in a Seattle council race," Wyble said. "The PAC can't keep its own donor list straight, and the people who put up most of the money won't say who they are. District 5 voters deserve to know who's paying to fill their mailboxes, and they deserve to know before they vote."

Interestingly, a major funnel of this dark money was Seattle's former Council president who lost her seat in a 2025 election drubbing: "SeaFor is a 501(c)(4) formed by former Councilmember Sara Nelson. It is not registered with the PDC or SEEC and does not disclose its donors," the Jenks campaign noted. "According to PubliCola, its website pitched the structure as protecting 'the privacy of businesses and individuals.'"

After the Jenks campaign filed its complaint and publications like PubliCola reported on it , the pro-Kang PAC said it returned the $30,000 donation from Nelson's SeaFor group. The PAC already spent the money on mailers so returning the check that accounted for two thirds of its fundraising has sunk it into debt, forcing it to ramp up fundraising – potentially to the same donors using SeaFor.

Without the SeaFor smoke screen to hide behind, the donors will eventually be revealed, although likely not until after ballot boxes close. The contributors that North Seattle Neighbors does list include former interim Seattle Mayor Tim Burgess and several real estate bigshots including Vulcan's chief real estate officer Ada Healey, Fremont land baron Suzie Burke, and Judith Runstad.

Nelson has indicated that SeaFor's 2026 spends are a test run on a broader 2027 strategy to keep control of Seattle Council in centrist hands – currently Council's progressive wing has just three members, while six councilmembers are some shade of centrist.

The other major endeavor SeaFor is engaged in: running a website built on AI-slop city hall "reporting." The website appears geared toward galvanizing more conservative leaning folks to submit comments to Council.

It remains to be seen whether Nelson and her friends will need to pull off a D5 comeback to provide a proof of concept to megadonors on their dark money project, or whether simply keeping it fairly close will be proof enough. The 2027 council elections are likely to involve big spending, either way, if recent elections are any indication.

Political cartoonist and comedian Brett Hamil argued letting Nelson get away with this scheme would set a dangerous precedent: “Sara Nelson, Tanya Woo & the Julie Kang PAC (“North Seattle Neighbors”) are in the midst of the biggest campaign finance scandal possibly ever in Seattle, and if they face no serious consequences they will run the same playbook for seven city council seats next year.”

The PAC attacks have focused on Jenks' opposition to expanding CCTV camera surveillance and stay out orders for prostitution and public drug use, which she says is based on evidence that those approaches are not effective. Jenks has portrayed public safety as a top priority , but she has emphasized expanding the role of the civilian-run Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) department to boost safety. The question remains of whether surveillance cameras, stay out orders, and some vague police defunding insinuations are salient enough issues to swing voters, or whether voters view public safety from a broader and more nuanced perspective.

For now, most centrist councilmembers appear intent on kneecapping a good chunk of Mayor Katie Wilson's agenda and taking opportunistic political swings at her. Speculation is swirling at city hall that several councilmembers are mulling runs against the mayor when her seat is up in 2029. District-based members would need to survive 2027 reelection bids first unless they want to try pulling a Bruce Harrell and taking two years off from elected office before rebranding as an outsider.
Would the entry of Nilu Jenks shake up this dynamic or simply have centrist doubling down?
Bus funding increases are also on the ballot in Seattle and in Pierce County.

If voters approve it, the Seattle Transit Measure will renew existing bus service support and provide an additional 95,000 bus trips per year to boost service frequency on at least 10 routes . The measure also supports reduced fare programs for low-income residents.

Pierce County's measure , meanwhile, would be an even larger jump in bus investment, boosting Pierce Transit service by 47%. This would put Pierce County in closer parity with its neighbors after more than a decade of failing to approve a transit measure.

The Seattle measure appears likely to pass given the margins recent tax measures have run up in the Emerald City – and passage could give Mayor Katie Wilson some additional momentum building on her recent success speeding up Route 8 for bus riders.

Good news gaining another progressive ally on council and passing a major transit measure could act as a bit of a reset for the mayor – with some local media outlets still fixated on her handling of the fatal Bite of Seattle shooting, even more than three months after the fact.

If progressive seize control of Council in 2027, much larger policy swings would be on the table for Seattle's first progressive mayor in more than a decade. The first step is winning the opening skirmish in 2026.

articles.title: In Battle with Fire Department, Queen Anne Residents Win Parking Victory
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A quiet Queen Anne street has become a battleground between the Seattle Fire Department, residents wanting to park their cars, and the simple laws of geometry, but it looks to be Seattle's own parking regulations that have lost the battle – for now.

For decades, there's been an intermittent problem along the upper portion of 14th Avenue W, near Interbay along the west slope of Queen Anne Hill. The street is only around 15 feet wide, narrowing to as little as 14 feet and eight inches. With a row of on-street parking for residents, that isn't usually wide enough for a Seattle Fire Department ladder truck to easily pass through, depending on the exact width of the parked cars. Either the fire truck operator needs to inch their way down 14th to ensure no parked cars get hit, or they need to find another route.

Earlier this year, at the fire department's urging, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) announced that the street would be entering a new era, with on-street parking prohibited to improve Seattle Fire Department (SFD) response times.

"For every minute we are delayed getting to a fire, roughly that fire doubles in size, and so that increases the risk to you all," Seattle Fire Captain Tim Taylor, based out of Greenwood's Station 21, told Queen Anne residents at a community meeting held on the change this May. "When a rig can't get through or has to try to negotiate a very tight space, those are all things that are going to count directly against patient outcomes. That's the reality that we're dealing with."
Taylor noted that SFD had responded to these specific 14th Avenue blocks 73 times between the beginning of 2022 and this past March.

"We have six documented times where they took the time to send updates to the battalion chiefs and to leadership saying: 'Hey, we had a significant delay due to vehicles blocking and parking on this block,'" Taylor said. "I can tell you, I run into delays quite often. Just traffic or whatever, I don't often take the time to document it. It has to be pretty important for me to take the time to actually send the documentation that we were delayed on a response."

The idea of making parking adjustments to improve public safety might be expected to be non-controversial, but at the May community meeting, the pushback on the change was intense. Residents along 14th repeatedly pressed city staff on finding another path forward, with things turning so combative that one attendee had to be asked to leave after presenting an obscene hand gesture to city staff.
Though the discussion had been arranged to hear residents' concerns about the new parking restrictions, an expectation was laid out at the top: this adjustment was moving forward.
"I do find that it is very important to state at the beginning, this decision is not going to be changed," Rebecca Duran, executive aide to District 7 Councilmember Bob Kettle, told attendees.

And yet, just a few months later, SDOT announced that the decision had in fact been changed. A six-month pilot will evaluate whether vehicles can remain parked on the street "as long as they fit within the available right of way without interfering with reliable emergency vehicle access." A painted line has been added to the length of the street, with signs directing drivers to only park between the line and the curb.

"If your vehicle does not fit the marked area, you can’t park," SDOT's website on the change states. "Together with SFD, we’ll monitor how well the new design supports reliable emergency vehicles’ access. The results will help inform next steps."

On a recent visit to the street, The Urbanist found parked vehicles that were all within the constraints of the painted line on the street – even if that meant that a significant portion of their vehicle was up on the curb. That's also not allowed under the rules of the pilot, which state vehicles have to be 62 inches wide or less to be able to park on the street.
During that May meeting, residents pleaded with the SDOT planner present to essentially grant permission to park on the curb, but were rebuffed.

"The curbs are not actually designed to hold the weight of your vehicle, so you can end up damaging that and the underlaying structure if you park on the wall," SDOT Deputy Transportation Operations Director Matt Beaulieu said that night.

Getting questions answered about how this new parking scheme will be determined to be a success involved a lot of finger pointing within City departments. SDOT referred questions from The Urbanist to the Seattle Fire Department, which then noted that the Seattle Police Department is in charge of parking enforcement.

"Standard parking enforcement practices led by Seattle Police will be in effect. Seattle Fire has no role in enforcement," SFD spokesperson Kim Schmanke wrote. "Seattle Fire will evaluate delays to responses along the route due to access issues and if there were any reported obstructions noted during the non-emergency times."

SPD's parking enforcement division is not as well-resourced as other areas of the police department, with Mayor Katie Wilson recently proposing to eliminate several parking officer positions that had been sitting unfilled for several years. Most of the parking enforcement officer (PEO) resources are focused on areas of the city that have paid parking programs, or in responding to complaints as directed by other officers. With paid parking set to expand to Upper Queen Anne and Alaska Junction, that could mean even less resources for parking enforcement in other areas of the city.

With SFD evaluating response times and SPD maintaining control over enforcement, the pilot appears set up in a way that implicitly condones parking on the curb. But another precedent is potentially being set here, and that concerns SFD's requirements around fire lanes. With some exceptions, Seattle's current fire code requires access roads used by fire department vehicles to have an "unobstructed width" of not less than 20 feet.

But that standard is clearly not being met on 14th Avenue W, which if explicitly acknowledged within City bureaucracy could open the door to more flexible designs elsewhere, clearing a path for greater pedestrianization and traffic calming interventions. In the UK, a fire lane access road is generally only required to be around 12 feet.
"Seattle Fire agreed to this pilot knowing the constraints of the road width and SDOT’s capabilities," Schmanke wrote.

Depending on the way this pilot plays out, the results could have wide-ranging impacts beyond the sleepy confines of 14th Avenue W. For now, drivers will be able to park their cars, regardless of whether doing so involves going up on the curb.

articles.title: Sunday Video: How Does Philadelphia Even Exist
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Shortly after his visit to Seattle (where he attending a talk co-hosted by with The Urbanist), Ray Delahanty headed to the East Coast and did a similar event in Philadelphia. Ray had a lot to say about Philly's walkability and other positive aspects that often fly under the radar, sandwiched as the city is between New York City and Washington D.C., which have higher profiles nationally and internationally.

Delahanty declared Philadelphia might have the most walkable city core in the whole United States, which stems in large part from the thoughtful urban plan William Penn made for the city as he founded it in 1682, with plenty of narrow streets friendly to pedestrians.

"These streets are really a microcosm of what I'm thinking about when I think about walkability," Delahanty said. "It's not just about the physical act of walking. It's how a street handles motor vehicles. It's whether the streetscape is visually interesting. It's whether you feel secure. It's whether there are a ton of destinations nearby that are worth walking to."
Philadelphia – at least in the center city and South Philly neighborhoods that Ray explored – checked all those boxes. These distinctions puts it among North America's most walkable cities.

It's not all roses in the City of Brotherly Love. Philadelphia is also dealing with service cuts on SEPTA, a legacy metro system which has an impressive network of rapid transit lines across the region. As Delahanty highlighted, those cuts mean frequencies have decreased, especially on weekends, when even bedrock routes are now seeing mediocre 10-minute headways – not really in line with a top-tier transit city, which boasts a population of 1.5 million, amid a metropolitan region of 6.3 million. Hopefully SEPTA can get out of its downward spiral and back on the path of service improvements and growth.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: ORCA Survey
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The ORCA consortium has a survey asking users about their experiences using ORCA cards and the fare payment system. The survey is open until mid November. The Friday Roundtable column is for short, light, interactive topics, so this is an opportunity to ask readers the same question: how is your experience using ORCA cards and the fare payment system in general?

There are several aspects to consider. There’s tapping an ORCA card, or using a credit card with the new open-payment system for credit cards. Using the readers may be better or worse on Link, regular buses, RapidRide, or Sounder. There’s obtaining the card and refilling it, at a ticket vending machine (TVM), at the MyORCA.com website, or getting a card mailed to you. There’s customer service offices. There’s the fare structure, and free transfers. There’s the times you have to explain the system to visitors or occasional riders at the platform or bus stop when it’s not obvious to them. And probably many other things.
My two biggest issues with ORCA are the time it takes to register a tap, and paying for part of a pass with an e-purse.

When you hold an ORCA card to a reader, the second-generation system takes twice as long to register a tap than the previous system did. So on buses I either have to hold up the line behind me, or tap and leave and assume it will either beep while I’m walking away or it won’t beep and I’ll get a free ride.

The second issue is when you want to split a pass cost between e-purse and a credit card. I switched to e-purse during the pandemic, and back to a pass this year. In the past at TVMs I’ve been able to use the $60 e-purse value for partial payment for the $108 pass, and pay the rest by credit card. I’d then have to do a second credit-card payment to put $10 back into the e-purse for occasional surcharges, because it had no option to take just $50 out of the e-purse and leave the other $10.

This year when I went back to using passes, the TVM wouldn’t even do that. The e-purse option was disabled, so the only choices were credit card or cash. That’s presumably because the e-purse value wasn’t enough for the entire pass. I didn’t want to leave $60 in the e-purse unused forever, so I went to Metro’s customer service office to make the kind of payment split I wanted. It would be nice if the TVMs could do this.

articles.title: Sound Transit Pilots Updated Pet Policy
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Sound Transit is piloting an updated pet policy on its buses and trains between now and Spring 2027. During the pilot, pet dogs will be permitted on board if they are leashed, well-behaved, and controlled by their handler. All other pets must remain in an enclosed carrier. As always, service animals are permitted in compliance with the ADA.

Prior to the pilot, dogs and other pets were only allowed on Sound Transit buses and trains in a carrier. In July 2025, the Sound Transit Board approved Motion No. M2025-34 , directing the agency to consider updating the rules to allow leashed dogs. This motion was motivated by the opening of Marymoor Village station as part of the Downtown Redmond Link Extension in May 2025. Marymoor Village station is next to Marymoor Park, a 640-arce park which includes a 40-arce off-leash dog area.

Will this pilot impact the passenger experience on Sound Transit? Probably not. In a presentation to the Executive Committee before the motion was approved, then-Acting Executive Director of Security & Fare Engagement Brian de Place acknowledged that passengers already take leashed dogs on Sound Transit buses and trains. While doing so did violate the rules, de Place noted “if the dog is leashed and generally under control, security will not engage with that passenger unless there is an actual disturbance”. In the year prior to this meeting, Sound Transit security only received 8 calls about pets.
There are few other notes pet owners should be aware of before bringing their leashed dogs onboard:
If you encounter an aggressive animal or other issues, call or text Sound Transit security: (206) 398-5268. In an emergency, call 911.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
